claim: Eight subtypes of T4/T5 neurons are defined by combinations of two patterns of dendritic inputs and four patterns of axonal outputs.
source: Eight subtypes of T4/T5 neurons are defined by combinations of two patterns of dendritic inputs and four patterns of axonal outputs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the morphological descriptions and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Single-cell profiling during development revealed distinct transcriptional programs defining each dendrite and axon wiring pattern.
source: Single-cell profiling during development revealed distinct transcriptional programs defining each dendrite and axon wiring pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript, including clustering analysis and differential gene expression.

claim: These programs were defined by the expression of a few transcription factors and different combinations of cell surface proteins.
source: These programs were defined by the expression of a few transcription factors and different combinations of cell surface proteins.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing specific TFs (bi, grn, TfAP-2) and CSPs associated with different wiring patterns.

claim: Gain and loss of function studies provide evidence for independent control of different wiring features.
source: Gain and loss of function studies provide evidence for independent control of different wiring features.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from RNAi and overexpression experiments, particularly for grn.

claim: Modular transcriptional programs for distinct wiring features are assembled in different combinations to generate diverse patterns of neuronal connectivity.
source: We propose that modular transcriptional programs for distinct wiring features are assembled in different combinations to generate diverse patterns of neuronal connectivity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the integration of transcriptional profiling and functional studies.

claim: T4/T5 neurons share a common developmental origin, physiological function, and general morphology, but differ in their precise wiring patterns and preferred stimulus.
source: T4/T5 neurons share a common developmental origin, physiological function, and general morphology, but differ in their precise wiring patterns and preferred stimulus (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Maisak et al., 2013; Apitz and Salecker, 2018; Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2018; Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are eight morphological subtypes of T4/T5 neurons in each column of the lobula plate (LoP) neuropil.
source: There are eight morphological subtypes of T4/T5 neurons in each column of the lobula plate (LoP) neuropil (see below), comprising the most abundant cell type in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the morphological descriptions and figures.

claim: The four T4 subtypes share a common set of dendritic inputs in the medulla.
source: These subtypes can be classified into two quartets of subtypes based on dendritic inputs: the four T4 subtypes share a common set of dendritic inputs in the medulla, and the four T5 subtypes share a different set of dendritic inputs in the lobula (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The four T5 subtypes share a different set of dendritic inputs in the lobula.
source: These subtypes can be classified into two quartets of subtypes based on dendritic inputs: the four T4 subtypes share a common set of dendritic inputs in the medulla, and the four T5 subtypes share a different set of dendritic inputs in the lobula (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: T4 neurons respond to ON stimuli (i.e. bright edges moving against a dark background).
source: T4 neurons respond to ON stimuli (i.e. bright edges moving against a dark background) and T5 to OFF stimuli (i.e. dark edges moving across a bright background).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge about T4/T5 neurons.

claim: T5 neurons respond to OFF stimuli (i.e. dark edges moving across a bright background).
source: T4 neurons respond to ON stimuli (i.e. bright edges moving against a dark background) and T5 to OFF stimuli (i.e. dark edges moving across a bright background).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge about T4/T5 neurons.

claim: T4/T5 neurons can be classified into four pairs of subtypes (a-d) based on the location of their axon terminals within a given column in layers a-d of the LoP.
source: T4/T5 neurons can also be classified into four pairs of subtypes (a-d) based on the location of their axon terminals within a given column in layers a-d of the LoP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in the figures.

claim: Each pair of T4/T5 subtypes responds selectively to visual motion in one of four cardinal directions: posterior, anterior, upwards, and downwards, respectively.
source: Each pair responds selectively to visual motion in one of four cardinal directions: posterior, anterior, upwards, and downwards, respectively (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge about T4/T5 neurons.

claim: Transcriptional profiling of the adult Drosophila brain revealed a common transcriptional signature for all T4/T5 neurons.
source: Although transcriptional profiling of the adult Drosophila brain revealed a common transcriptional signature for all T4/T5 neurons, genetic programs for individual subtypes have not been identified (Davie et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic programs for individual T4/T5 subtypes have not been identified prior to this study.
source: Although transcriptional profiling of the adult Drosophila brain revealed a common transcriptional signature for all T4/T5 neurons, genetic programs for individual subtypes have not been identified (Davie et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and sets up the motivation for the current work.

claim: Sequencing was performed at 48 hr after puparium formation (APF).
source: Sequencing was performed at 48 hr after puparium formation (APF).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: 48 hr APF precedes a period of widespread synaptogenesis in the visual system.
source: This developmental time point precedes a period of widespread synaptogenesis in the visual system, and coincides with the appearance of four discrete synaptic layers (a, b, c, d) in the LoP neuropil.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and provides context for the developmental timing.

claim: 48 hr APF coincides with the appearance of four discrete synaptic layers (a, b, c, d) in the LoP neuropil.
source: This developmental time point precedes a period of widespread synaptogenesis in the visual system, and coincides with the appearance of four discrete synaptic layers (a, b, c, d) in the LoP neuropil.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and provides context for the developmental timing.

claim: RNA-Seq libraries were generated using 10X Chromium technology.
source: RNA-Seq libraries were generated using Chromium Single Cell Reagent Kit V2 according to the manufacturer's protocol, with 12 cycles of PCR for cDNA amplification.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The final dataset consisted of 3557 cells with 1000–2000 genes per cell at 48 hr APF.
source: After quality control and removal of outlier cells, our final dataset consisted of 3557 cells with 1000–2000 genes per cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the data processing.

claim: Unsupervised analysis revealed eight clusters of approximately equal numbers of cells.
source: Unsupervised analysis revealed eight clusters of approximately equal numbers of cells (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that each cluster corresponded to a single T4/T5 subtype.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Each cluster corresponded to a single T4/T5 subtype.
source: Unsupervised analysis revealed eight clusters of approximately equal numbers of cells (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that each cluster corresponded to a single T4/T5 subtype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of eight clusters matching the known eight subtypes.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 69 genes which were strongly expressed in some clusters and not in others.
source: This revealed 69 genes which were strongly expressed in some clusters and not in others.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the differential expression analysis.

claim: Cluster-enriched genes were not specific to single clusters.
source: Cluster-enriched genes, however, were not specific to single clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Each of the five subtypes of lamina neurons is defined by at least one subtype-type specific transcription factor.
source: By contrast, for instance, each of the five subtypes of lamina neurons is defined by at least one subtype-type specific transcription factor (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and provides a contrast to the T4/T5 findings.

claim: T4/T5 subtypes separated into eight transcriptionally distinct clusters, but were not defined by unique molecular markers.
source: Thus, while T4/T5 subtypes separated into eight transcriptionally distinct clusters, they were not defined by unique molecular markers (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Three independent components (ICs) each split the eight T4/T5 clusters into two groups of four, each in a different way.
source: Intriguingly, three independent components (ICs) each split the eight T4/T5 clusters into two groups of four, each in a different way (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Three ICs were sufficient to define all eight clusters.
source: Together, these three ICs were sufficient to define all eight clusters (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Each of the three ICs defined an axis of transcriptional diversity driven by a group of genes differentially expressed along each axis.
source: Each of the three ICs defined an axis of transcriptional diversity (hereafter referred to as Axis 1, 2, 3) driven by a group of genes differentially expressed along each axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of ICs.

claim: Many genes associated with the three axes were expressed in a binary (ON/OFF) pattern in one of the two groups of clusters separated along each axis.
source: Many of these genes were expressed in a binary (ON/OFF) pattern in one of the two groups of clusters separated along each axis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Binary expression of bifid (bi) defined the two groups of clusters separated by Axis 1.
source: Binary expression of bifid (bi) defined the two groups of clusters separated by Axis 1, grain (grn) defined the clusters separated by Axis 2, and TfAP-2 defined the clusters separated by Axis 3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Binary expression of grain (grn) defined the clusters separated by Axis 2.
source: Binary expression of bifid (bi) defined the two groups of clusters separated by Axis 1, grain (grn) defined the clusters separated by Axis 2, and TfAP-2 defined the clusters separated by Axis 3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Binary expression of TfAP-2 defined the clusters separated by Axis 3.
source: Binary expression of bifid (bi) defined the two groups of clusters separated by Axis 1, grain (grn) defined the clusters separated by Axis 2, and TfAP-2 defined the clusters separated by Axis 3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Each cluster expresses a unique combination of genes.
source: Thus, while no individual cluster is uniquely defined by the expression of a single gene, each cluster expresses a unique combination of genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Three axes of diversity with orthogonal ON/OFF expression patterns of TFs define the eight T4/T5 clusters.
source: In this way, three axes of diversity with orthogonal ON/OFF expression patterns of TFs define the eight T4/T5 clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a summary of the findings.

claim: Axis 1 separated clusters into two groups of four that were defined by mutually exclusive binary expression of Fasciclin 2 (Fas2) and klingon (klg).
source: Axis 1 separated clusters into two groups of four that were defined by mutually exclusive binary expression of two genes, Fasciclin 2 (Fas2) and klingon (klg), respectively (Figure 3A), each encoding immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fas2 was expressed in LoP layers a/b.
source: Fas2 was expressed in LoP layers a/b, whereas klg was expressed in LoP layers c/d (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: klg was expressed in LoP layers c/d.
source: Fas2 was expressed in LoP layers a/b, whereas klg was expressed in LoP layers c/d (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Clusters expressing Fas2 and klg also expressed previously described markers for T4/T5 subtypes a/b (dachshund (dac)) and c/d (bi, Connectin (Con)).
source: Clusters expressing Fas2 and klg also expressed previously described markers for T4/T5 subtypes a/b (dachshund (dac)) and c/d (bi, Connectin (Con)) (Apitz and Salecker, 2018) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, with citation to previous work.

claim: Axis 1 separated LoP layer a/b and c/d subtypes, defining specificity of axonal outputs between two broad domains of the LoP.
source: Thus, Axis 1 separated LoP layer a/b and c/d subtypes, defining specificity of axonal outputs between two broad domains of the LoP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Axis 1 corresponds to separation of horizontal (posterior/anterior) and vertical (upwards/downwards) motion detection circuits.
source: This corresponds to separation of horizontal (posterior/anterior) and vertical (upwards/downwards) motion detection circuits, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the Axis 1 separation.

claim: Axis 2 separated clusters into two groups of four defined by binary expression of beat-IV and the TF grn.
source: Axis 2 separated clusters into two groups of four defined by binary expression of beat-IV (an Ig superfamily protein) and the TF grn.
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: Both beat-IV and grn were expressed in LoP layers b/c, but not a/d.
source: Both genes were expressed in LoP layers b/c, but not a/d.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Axis 2 separated subtypes into inner (b and c) and outer (a and d) LoP layer subtypes in a symmetrical fashion, defining specificity of axonal outputs between adjacent layers within the two broad domains of the LoP.
source: Thus, Axis 2 further separated subtypes into inner (b and c) and outer (a and d) LoP layer subtypes in a symmetrical fashion, defining specificity of axonal outputs between adjacent layers within the two broad domains of the LoP (Figure 3A'–3C').
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Axis 2 corresponds to further separation of each of the motion detection circuits into two subcircuits detecting motion in two opposing directions.
source: This corresponds to further separation of each of the motion detection circuits into two subcircuits detecting motion in two opposing directions (i.e. horizontal into posterior and anterior, and vertical into upwards and downwards motion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the Axis 2 separation.

claim: Axis 3 separated clusters into two groups of four defined by binary expression of dpr2 and beat-VI, each encoding an Ig superfamily protein.
source: Axis 3 separated clusters into two groups of four defined by binary expression of dpr2 and beat-VI, each encoding an Ig superfamily protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: Both dpr2 and beat-VI were expressed in all LoP layers, and M10 but not Lo1.
source: In vivo, both genes were expressed in all LoP layers, and M10 but not Lo1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Axis 3 separated all T4 from all T5 subtypes, defining specificity of dendritic inputs.
source: Thus, Axis 3 separated all T4 from all T5 subtypes, defining specificity of dendritic inputs (Figure 3A''–3C'').
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Axis 3 corresponds to separation into two parallel circuits for ON and OFF motion detection.
source: This corresponds to separation into two parallel circuits for ON and OFF motion detection, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the Axis 3 separation.

claim: A combination of Axis 1 and Axis 2 defined four types of axonal outputs (a, b, c, d).
source: A combination of Axis 1 and Axis 2 defined four types of axonal outputs (a, b, c, d), and Axis 3 defined two types of dendritic inputs (T4 and T5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a summary of the findings.

claim: Axis 3 defined two types of dendritic inputs (T4 and T5).
source: A combination of Axis 1 and Axis 2 defined four types of axonal outputs (a, b, c, d), and Axis 3 defined two types of dendritic inputs (T4 and T5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a summary of the findings.

claim: Comparison of T4a to T4c or T4d, which have axonal outputs in non-adjacent LoP layers, yielded the largest number of differentially expressed genes (58 and 55, respectively).
source: Comparison of T4a to T4c or T4d, which have axonal outputs in non-adjacent LoP layers, yielded the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs, 58 and 55, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pairwise comparisons.

claim: T4a and T4b have axonal outputs in adjacent LoP layers, and were separated by an intermediate number of DEGs (16).
source: T4a and T4b have axonal outputs in adjacent LoP layers, and were separated by an intermediate number of DEGs (16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pairwise comparisons.

claim: Only a small number of DEGs (9) separated T4a and T5a, which share axonal output but receive different dendritic inputs.
source: Finally, only a small number of DEGs (9) separated T4a and T5a, which share axonal output but receive different dendritic inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing pairwise comparisons.

claim: Virtually all DEGs were co-regulated across all subtypes according to either specificity of axonal outputs or dendritic inputs.
source: Expression patterns of the DEGs from pairwise comparisons across all T4/T5 subtypes revealed a general pattern (Figure 4, lower dot plots): virtually all DEGs were co-regulated across all subtypes according to either specificity of axonal outputs or dendritic inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Distinct sets of DEGs were expressed in each pair of subtypes with shared axonal outputs, but different dendritic inputs.
source: In other words, distinct sets of DEGs were expressed in each pair of subtypes with shared axonal outputs, but different dendritic inputs (e.g. in T4a and T5a, Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: A distinct set of DEGs was expressed in groups of subtypes with shared dendritic inputs, but different axonal outputs (i.e. all T4 subtypes).
source: Similarly, a distinct set of DEGs was expressed in groups of subtypes with shared dendritic inputs, but different axonal outputs (i.e. all T4 subtypes, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Many of the DEGs have been implicated in neuronal wiring specificity.
source: Many of the DEGs have been implicated in neuronal wiring specificity (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: Approximately half of the DEGs encoded CSPs with cell adhesion domains (Ig/LRR), including multiple members of the dpr/DIP and beat/side families of interacting proteins.
source: Approximately half of the DEGs encoded CSPs with cell adhesion domains (Ig/LRR), including multiple members of the dpr/DIP and beat/side families of interacting proteins (Zinn and Özkan, 2017); specific members of these families have been shown to regulate axon guidance and synaptic specificity in the developing fly nervous system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation to previous work.

claim: Specific members of the dpr/DIP and beat/side families have been shown to regulate axon guidance and synaptic specificity in the developing fly nervous system.
source: Approximately half of the DEGs encoded CSPs with cell adhesion domains (Ig/LRR), including multiple members of the dpr/DIP and beat/side families of interacting proteins (Zinn and Özkan, 2017); specific members of these families have been shown to regulate axon guidance and synaptic specificity in the developing fly nervous system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation to previous work.

claim: The transcriptional organization of T4/T5 neurons mirrored their wiring patterns.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that the transcriptional organization of T4/T5 neurons mirrored their wiring patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: Discrete groups of co-regulated genes reiteratively defined either shared axon or shared dendrite wiring patterns among different subtypes.
source: Discrete groups of co-regulated genes reiteratively defined either shared axon or shared dendrite wiring patterns among different subtypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: These groups of genes were assembled in different combinations to uniquely define the eight T4/T5 subtypes.
source: These groups of genes were assembled in different combinations to uniquely define the eight T4/T5 subtypes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: At 24 hr APF, eight distinct populations were identified separated by three equivalent axes of transcriptional diversity.
source: Similar to our dataset at 48 hr APF, we identified eight distinct populations separated by three equivalent axes of transcriptional diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the 24 hr APF dataset.

claim: Many of the same genes were associated with the three axes at both 24 hr and 48 hr APF.
source: Many of the same genes were associated with these axes at both time points, allowing us to match subtypes between 24 hr and 48 hr APF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TFs defining the primary axes of diversity (bi, grn, TfAP-2) were expressed in the same sets of subtypes at both 24 hr and 48 hr APF.
source: TFs defining the primary axes of diversity (bi, grn, TfAP-2) were expressed in the same sets of subtypes at both time points, suggesting they may contribute to stable subtype identities during development (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Some CSPs exhibited stable expression, marking subtypes with shared axon or dendrite wiring patterns at both time points.
source: Some CSPs also exhibited stable expression, marking subtypes with shared axon or dendrite wiring patterns at both time points.
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: Other CSPs were dynamically regulated and were specific to subtypes only at a particular stage of development.
source: Other CSPs were dynamically regulated and were specific to subtypes only at a particular stage of development (Figure 5B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dynamic changes in gene expression were coordinated among subtypes with shared wiring features.
source: Interestingly, dynamic changes in gene expression were also coordinated among subtypes with shared wiring features (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: dpr3 and a few other CSPs were synchronously upregulated in all T4 subtypes from 24 hr to 48 hr APF.
source: For example, dpr3 and a few other CSPs were synchronously upregulated in all T4 subtypes from 24 hr to 48 hr APF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an example of coordinated gene expression.

claim: Toll-6 was synchronously upregulated in both LoP layer 'a' subtypes (T4a/T5a).
source: Similarly, Toll-6 was synchronously upregulated in both LoP layer 'a' subtypes (T4a/T5a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an example of coordinated gene expression.

claim: Similar transcriptional programs unfold in parallel among T4/T5 subtypes with shared wiring features.
source: These data indicate that similar transcriptional programs unfold in parallel among T4/T5 subtypes with shared wiring features.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the developmental analysis.

claim: During the period covered in the study (24–48 hr APF) four LoP layers form in two discrete lamination steps.
source: During the period covered in our study (24–48 hr APF) four LoP layers form in two discrete lamination steps (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The T4/T5 axon terminals first laminate into two broad domains corresponding to layers a/b and c/d.
source: The T4/T5 axon terminals first laminate into two broad domains corresponding to layers a/b and c/d.
evidence: This is stated in the Results describing the lamination process.

claim: The two broad domains then further sublaminate into two pairs of adjacent layers to form the four discrete LoP layers, a, b, c, and d.
source: These domains then further sublaminate into two pairs of adjacent layers to form the four discrete LoP layers, a, b, c, and d.
evidence: This is stated in the Results describing the lamination process.

claim: The two primary axes of transcriptional diversity mirrored the two stages of LoP layer formation.
source: The two primary axes of transcriptional diversity mirrored these two stages of LoP layer formation, suggesting a regulatory code for axon wiring (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutually exclusive expression of the TFs dac and bi/pros separated a/b (dac+) from c/d (bi+/pros+) subtypes.
source: Mutually exclusive expression of the TFs dac and bi/pros separated a/b (dac+) from c/d (bi+/pros+) subtypes (i.e. Axis 1, Apitz and Salecker, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of the TF grn separated subtypes into inner (b and c, grn+) and outer (a and d, grn-) layer subtypes in a symmetrical fashion.
source: These subtypes were further separated by expression of the TF grn into inner (b and c, grn+) and outer (a and d, grn-) layer subtypes in a symmetrical fashion (i.e. Axis 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: RNAi of bi in all T4/T5 neurons results in loss of the c/d domain of the LoP.
source: RNAi of bi in all T4/T5 neurons results in loss of the c/d domain of the LoP, whereas overexpression results in loss of the a/b domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of bi results in loss of the a/b domain of the LoP.
source: RNAi of bi in all T4/T5 neurons results in loss of the c/d domain of the LoP, whereas overexpression results in loss of the a/b domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation to previous work.

claim: In both RNAi and overexpression of bi, further sublamination of remaining inner and outer LoP layer pairs still occurs.
source: In both cases, further sublamination of remaining inner and outer LoP layer pairs still occurs (Apitz and Salecker, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation to previous work.

claim: RNAi of grn resulted in distinct a/b and c/d LoP domains still being separated by a pronounced gap and differential expression of Con, but both domains failed to sublaminate into inner and outer layers.
source: We performed RNAi of grn, which resulted in a different phenotype; whereas distinct a/b and c/d LoP domains were still separated by a pronounced gap and differential expression of Con (a marker for LoP layers c/d), both domains failed to sublaminate into inner and outer layers, instead forming a single layer each (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The overall morphological organization of T4/T5 neurons was otherwise unaffected by grn RNAi.
source: The overall morphological organization of T4/T5 neurons was otherwise unaffected.
evidence: This is stated in the Results describing the grn RNAi phenotype.

claim: Overexpression of grn in all T4/T5 neurons resulted in a specific failure of a/b and c/d LoP domains to sublaminate.
source: Overexpression of grn in all T4/T5 neurons also resulted in a specific failure of a/b and c/d LoP domains to sublaminate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: RNAi and overexpression of grn resulted in significant loss of T4/T5 neuron numbers between 24 hr and 48 hr APF.
source: RNAi and overexpression of grn resulted in significant loss of T4/T5 neuron numbers between 24 hr and 48 hr APF (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), associated with an increase in apoptosis (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: RNAi and overexpression of grn were associated with an increase in apoptosis.
source: RNAi and overexpression of grn resulted in significant loss of T4/T5 neuron numbers between 24 hr and 48 hr APF (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), associated with an increase in apoptosis (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of baculovirus caspase inhibitor p35 in developing T4/T5s rescued cell death associated with grn overexpression.
source: Expression of baculovirus caspase inhibitor p35 in developing T4/T5s rescued cell death associated with grn overexpression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results.

claim: T4/T5 axons still failed to sublaminate into four discrete LoP layers when apoptosis was blocked by p35 expression during grn overexpression.
source: Nevertheless, T4/T5 axons still failed to sublaminate into four discrete LoP layers (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Differential expression of grn is specifically required for sublamination of T4/T5 axons between pairs of adjacent LoP layers.
source: Thus, differential expression of grn is specifically required for sublamination of T4/T5 axons between pairs of adjacent LoP layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the functional experiments.

claim: Axon-specific transcriptional programs defined by binary (ON/OFF) expression patterns of two TFs, bi and grn, control the formation of four LoP layers and corresponding T4/T5 axonal wiring patterns.
source: We conclude that axon-specific transcriptional programs defined by binary (ON/OFF) expression patterns of two TFs, bi and grn, control the formation of four LoP layers and corresponding T4/T5 axonal wiring patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as a conclusion from the functional experiments.

claim: Separable transcriptional programs correlate with specific wiring features of T4/T5 neurons.
source: Unsupervised analysis revealed that separable transcriptional programs correlate with these specific wiring features.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: These programs control specific axonal targeting features, which are separable from other features (e.g. dendrite targeting).
source: We demonstrate through gain and loss of function experiments that these programs control specific axonal targeting features, which are separable from other features (e.g. dendrite targeting).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: These programs can be re-assembled in a modular fashion to generate neuronal subtypes with different combinations of wiring features.
source: These programs can be re-assembled in a modular fashion to generate neuronal subtypes with different combinations of wiring features.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: A modular transcriptional architecture may provide a general strategy for discrete modifications to neuronal connectivity in development and evolution.
source: A modular transcriptional architecture may provide a general strategy for discrete modifications to neuronal connectivity in development and evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation about broader implications.

claim: A common T4/T5 neuronal identity is defined by a unique combination of TFs expressed in all subtypes (e.g. Lim1, Drgx, acj6).
source: A common T4/T5 neuronal identity is defined by a unique combination of TFs expressed in all subtypes (e.g. Lim1, Drgx, acj6) (Davie et al., 2018; Konstantinides et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Perturbation of TFs expressed in all subtypes disrupts overall organization of T4/T5 neurons, including both dendritic and axonal morphologies.
source: Perturbation of TFs expressed in all subtypes disrupts overall organization of T4/T5 neurons, including both dendritic and axonal morphologies (Contreras et al., 2018; Schilling et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The common T4/T5 transcriptional program is further diversified by separable feature-specific transcriptional programs.
source: We find that this common T4/T5 transcriptional program is further diversified by separable feature-specific transcriptional programs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Feature-specific programs are defined by three binary (ON/OFF) TF expression patterns, with two TF patterns defining the four axonal outputs and one TF pattern defining the two dendritic inputs.
source: These programs are defined by three binary (ON/OFF) TF expression patterns, with two TF patterns defining the four axonal outputs and one TF pattern defining the two dendritic inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Modular combinations of feature-specific TFs defining unique wiring patterns give rise to eight T4/T5 subtypes.
source: In this way, modular TF codes defining common and feature-specific transcriptional programs give rise to eight T4/T5 subtypes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Four pairs of T4/T5 subtypes with shared axonal outputs (and different dendritic inputs) each target one of four LoP layers, a-d.
source: Four pairs of T4/T5 subtypes with shared axonal outputs (and different dendritic inputs) each target one of four LoP layers, a-d.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The ultimate layered architecture of neuropils develops through sequential lamination into increasing numbers of layers.
source: The ultimate layered architecture of neuropils develops through sequential lamination into increasing numbers of layers (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010; Millard and Pecot, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Binary expression of bi is required for lamination of the broad a/b from c/d LoP domains.
source: Binary expression of bi is required for lamination of the broad a/b from c/d LoP domains (Apitz and Salecker, 2018), whereas binary expression of grn is required for sublamination of each of these two domains into separate LoP layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Binary expression of grn is required for sublamination of each of the two broad domains into separate LoP layers.
source: Binary expression of bi is required for lamination of the broad a/b from c/d LoP domains (Apitz and Salecker, 2018), whereas binary expression of grn is required for sublamination of each of these two domains into separate LoP layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Perturbation of each TF (bi or grn) exclusively disrupts the corresponding lamination step, while not affecting other morphological features of T4/T5 neurons.
source: Importantly, perturbation of each TF exclusively disrupts the corresponding lamination step, while not affecting other morphological features of T4/T5 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Two quartets of subtypes with shared dendritic inputs (and different axonal outputs) were defined by binary expression of TfAP-2.
source: Similarly, two quartets of subtypes with shared dendritic inputs (and different axonal outputs) were defined by binary expression of TfAP-2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Arborization of dendrites in M10 (T4) or Lo1 (T5) occurs during initial neurite guidance steps, preceding the developmental stages covered in this study.
source: Arborization of dendrites in M10 (T4) or Lo1 (T5) occurs during initial neurite guidance steps, preceding the developmental stages covered in this study (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: DEGs between T4 and T5 subtypes contribute to the connections with two distinct sets of presynaptic partners.
source: We hypothesize that DEGs between T4 and T5 subtypes identified in our analysis contribute to the connections with two distinct sets of presynaptic partners (Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis with citation to previous work.

claim: The binary expression patterns of TFs mirror the developmental lineages of T4/T5 neurons.
source: The binary expression patterns of TFs also mirror the developmental lineages of T4/T5 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: a/b and c/d subtypes arise from bi- and bi+ progenitor populations.
source: a/b and c/d subtypes arise from bi- and bi+ progenitor populations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Neuroblasts from each population undergo two terminal Notch-dependent asymmetric divisions to give rise to the eight subtypes.
source: Neuroblasts from each population undergo two terminal Notch-dependent asymmetric divisions to give rise to the eight subtypes (Pinto-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: These divisions correspond to binary expression patterns of grn and TfAP-2, which act with Notch signaling to regulate wiring.
source: These divisions correspond to binary expression patterns of grn and TfAP-2, respectively, which act with Notch signaling to regulate wiring.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Despite divergent developmental trajectories separated by multiple divisions and distinct progenitor pools, all T4 and all T5 subtypes converge onto the same transcriptional programs associated with two types of dendritic inputs.
source: Remarkably, despite divergent developmental trajectories separated by multiple divisions and distinct progenitor pools, all T4 and all T5 subtypes converge onto the same transcriptional programs associated with two types of dendritic inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claim: Three regulatory dichotomies could reflect the evolutionary origin of T4/T5 subtypes and correspond to consecutive duplications of ancestral cell types and circuits.
source: Three regulatory dichotomies could also reflect the evolutionary origin of T4/T5 subtypes and correspond to consecutive duplications of ancestral cell types and circuits (Shinomiya et al., 2015; Arendt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation with citations to previous work.

claim: Each axonal and dendritic transcriptional program is characterized by a specific pattern of TFs, as well as a set of CSPs, many of which are implicated in regulating wiring in other developmental contexts.
source: Each axonal and dendritic transcriptional program is characterized by a specific pattern of TFs, as well as a set of CSPs, many of which are implicated in regulating wiring in other developmental contexts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: Dynamic expression of CSPs in neurons with shared wiring features was developmentally coordinated.
source: Interestingly, dynamic expression of these proteins in neurons with shared wiring features was developmentally coordinated.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The synaptic specificity of T4/T5 dendrites and axons are determined by the combined activity of recognition molecules through interactions with synaptic partners.
source: We envision that the synaptic specificity of T4/T5 dendrites and axons are determined by the combined activity of these recognition molecules through interactions with synaptic partners.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: Combining separate dendritic and axonal programs, and variations on them, may contribute to the diversification of synaptic specificity in different neuronal subtypes across complex nervous systems.
source: Combining separate dendritic and axonal programs, and variations on them, may contribute to the diversification of synaptic specificity in different neuronal subtypes across complex nervous systems
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation about broader implications.

claim: T4/T5 neurons comprise the most abundant cell type in the fly visual system.
source: There are eight morphological subtypes of T4/T5 neurons in each column of the lobula plate (LoP) neuropil (see below), comprising the most abundant cell type in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Studies in both vertebrates and invertebrates have led to the identification of cell surface proteins (CSPs) that mediate selective association between neurites.
source: Studies in both vertebrates and invertebrates have led to the identification of cell surface proteins (CSPs) that mediate selective association between neurites (Tessier-Lavigne and Goodman, 1996; de Wit and Ghosh, 2016; Zinn and Özkan, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Gain and loss of function genetic studies have shown that combinations of different CSP families regulate specificity of neuronal connections.
source: Gain and loss of function genetic studies have shown that combinations of different CSP families regulate this specificity (Zarin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Neuronal subtypes express highly diverse repertoires of CSPs during circuit assembly.
source: Indeed, neuronal subtypes express highly diverse repertoires of CSPs during circuit assembly (Tan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017; Sarin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: Conserved regulatory strategies involving combinations of transcription factors (TFs) establish unique neuronal identities.
source: Conserved regulatory strategies involving combinations of transcription factors (TFs) establish unique neuronal identities (Allan and Thor, 2015; Enriquez et al., 2015; Hobert, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: The programs regulating expression of CSPs for specific neuronal wiring features are still poorly understood.
source: However, the programs regulating expression of CSPs for specific neuronal wiring features are still poorly understood.
